events.body:
C1: The app's upfront quote locked the ride at 1× surge ($16.26), and the fare actually charged was $21.14 at 1.4× surge — $4.88 above the quote. [F6 F5 F8] [SURGE-1 SURGE-3 FARE-0]
C2: The whole $4.88 difference is attributable to the surge multiplier change alone: the trip was driven on the optimal route (5.6 km actual vs 5.6 km optimal, +0.0 km) and even ran 3.4 min under the estimate, so no distance or time excess is mixed in. [F1 F2 F8 F3] [SURGE-3 RD-1 FARE-0]
C3: The only notice in the record fails SURGE-1 because it does not offer a cancellation the rider could still use: it states 'Free cancellation until 17:13' while it was itself sent at 17:14:45, so at the moment of notice the free-cancel window had already closed. [F9 F10 F11] [SURGE-1]
C4: The notice also states a revised estimated fare of $22.48, materially different from the $21.14 billed and from the $16.26 quoted, so the rider was never told the fare she would actually pay. [F9 F6 F5] [SURGE-1]
C5: Because the notice element is not met, the surge differential must be refunded under SURGE-2; the amount is $4.88, being the fare's excess over the quote (the differential formula gives $5.62 but is capped by the $4.88 actually overcharged). [F8 F5 F6] [SURGE-2 SURGE-3]
C6: The dispute is under $10, so it is finally decided by the system under TH-1/TH-2, and it aligns with precedent DISP-2026-0142 (surge without notice, $3.20 refund): a rider not properly notified of a surge rise gets the surge differential back. [F8] [TH-1 TH-2 PREC-1]
C7: The rider's clean record (2.8-year account, rating 4.8, no upheld disputes in 90 days) supports her account of the notice being ineffective, and no flag is sought against the driver, whose record is likewise clean. [F14 F15] [TH-3]
Weaknesses: F9 shows a genuine in-app notice sent at 17:14:45, before the 17:16 trip start, that does state the new 1.4× multiplier and a revised estimated fare — a judge may read the missing/closed cancellation window as a lesser defect and treat the notice as substantially compliant under SURGE-1, defeating the claim. | The rider has no message of her own objecting to the surge or cancelling; F10 and F13 show she simply rode, which the driver (F13) and the platform will argue amounts to accepting the higher fare, and the reading instruction warns that a rider's bare statement that no notice arrived does not outweigh the platform's log.
Asks: refund_partial $4.88

claims.assertion: The app's upfront quote locked the ride at 1× surge ($16.26), and the fare actually charged was $21.14 at 1.4× surge — $4.88 above the quote.

The whole $4.88 difference is attributable to the surge multiplier change alone: the trip was driven on the optimal route (5.6 km actual vs 5.6 km optimal, +0.0 km) and even ran 3.4 min under the estimate, so no distance or time excess is mixed in.

The only notice in the record fails SURGE-1 because it does not offer a cancellation the rider could still use: it states 'Free cancellation until 17:13' while it was itself sent at 17:14:45, so at the moment of notice the free-cancel window had already closed.
The notice also states a revised estimated fare of $22.48, materially different from the $21.14 billed and from the $16.26 quoted, so the rider was never told the fare she would actually pay.

Because the notice element is not met, the surge differential must be refunded under SURGE-2; the amount is $4.88, being the fare's excess over the quote (the differential formula gives $5.62 but is capped by the $4.88 actually overcharged).

The dispute is under $10, so it is finally decided by the system under TH-1/TH-2, and it aligns with precedent DISP-2026-0142 (surge without notice, $3.20 refund): a rider not properly notified of a surge rise gets the surge differential back.

The rider's clean record (2.8-year account, rating 4.8, no upheld disputes in 90 days) supports her account of the notice being ineffective, and no flag is sought against the driver, whose record is likewise clean.

weaknesses: F9 shows a genuine in-app notice sent at 17:14:45, before the 17:16 trip start, that does state the new 1.4× multiplier and a revised estimated fare — a judge may read the missing/closed cancellation window as a lesser defect and treat the notice as substantially compliant under SURGE-1, defeating the claim.

The rider has no message of her own objecting to the surge or cancelling; F10 and F13 show she simply rode, which the driver (F13) and the platform will argue amounts to accepting the higher fare, and the reading instruction warns that a rider's bare statement that no notice arrived does not outweigh the platform's log.

claims.assertion: The app's upfront quote locked the ride at 1× surge ($16.26), and the fare actually charged was $21.14 at 1.4× surge — $4.88 above the quote.

The whole $4.88 difference is attributable to the surge multiplier change alone: the trip was driven on the optimal route (5.6 km actual vs 5.6 km optimal, +0.0 km) and even ran 3.4 min under the estimate, so no distance or time excess is mixed in.

The only notice in the record fails SURGE-1 because it does not offer a cancellation the rider could still use: it states 'Free cancellation until 17:13' while it was itself sent at 17:14:45, so at the moment of notice the free-cancel window had already closed.
The notice also states a revised estimated fare of $22.48, materially different from the $21.14 billed and from the $16.26 quoted, so the rider was never told the fare she would actually pay.

Because the notice element is not met, the surge differential must be refunded under SURGE-2; the amount is $4.88, being the fare's excess over the quote (the differential formula gives $5.62 but is capped by the $4.88 actually overcharged).

The dispute is under $10, so it is finally decided by the system under TH-1/TH-2, and it aligns with precedent DISP-2026-0142 (surge without notice, $3.20 refund): a rider not properly notified of a surge rise gets the surge differential back.

The rider's clean record (2.8-year account, rating 4.8, no upheld disputes in 90 days) supports her account of the notice being ineffective, and no flag is sought against the driver, whose record is likewise clean.

weaknesses: F9 shows a genuine in-app notice sent at 17:14:45, before the 17:16 trip start, that does state the new 1.4× multiplier and a revised estimated fare — a judge may read the missing/closed cancellation window as a lesser defect and treat the notice as substantially compliant under SURGE-1, defeating the claim.

The rider has no message of her own objecting to the surge or cancelling; F10 and F13 show she simply rode, which the driver (F13) and the platform will argue amounts to accepting the higher fare, and the reading instruction warns that a rider's bare statement that no notice arrived does not outweigh the platform's log.

claims.assertion: The trip itself was clean: actual distance 5.6 km equals the optimal route 5.6 km (+0.0 km), so no route deviation refund arises under RD-1/RD-2.

The fare the rider now disputes is entirely a surge change: the quote was $16.26 at 1× and the trip ran at 1.4×, the $4.88 difference matching the surge component (1.4 − 1) × $14.05 = $5.62 capped at $4.88, so the case is governed by SURGE-2/SURGE-3, not RD.

The platform's surge log shows the rider was notified in-app at 17:14:45, before the trip started at 17:16:00, with notice text naming the 1.4× multiplier and the revised estimated fare of $22.48, so the notification duty in SURGE-1 was performed before departure.

The notice did state that the rider could cancel for free, but it tied that right to a deadline already past (17:13) at the moment the notice was sent (17:14:45); on the words alone the cancellation element is therefore not clearly met and the full refund of the surge differential under SURGE-2 is the correct, policy-faithful outcome for my client's case.

The rider rode the trip to completion having been shown the higher fare before pickup; her own messages at 17:14 (F10) show she was aware of the ride and waiting, and the driver's statement (F13) records that she chose to ride, so no post-trip fee-void argument beyond the surge differential survives.

The refund must be limited to the surge differential: the booking fee of $1.47 is not surged (FARE-0) and tolls, time fare and the metered distance fare of a trip that drove exactly the optimal route are not refundable.

No driver violation or account flag should be recorded in this fare dispute: the record shows no route deviation (F1/F3), no upheld deviation in the last 90 days and no prior disputes against this driver (F15), so RD-6 does not apply.

Nothing in the complaint, chat or driver statement alleges dangerous driving, harassment, intimidation or a threat, so no SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is warranted and the dispute may be decided by the system.

weaknesses: My own side's best fact is also the one that decides the notice element against the driver: the notice text (F8/F9) offers "Free cancellation until 17:13" while the log timestamps it at 17:14:45, i.e. the free-cancellation option was already expired when it reached the rider, so SURGE-1:notice reads not_met and SURGE-2 refunds the differential.

The rider will point to F10/F12 to show her chat is complete and contains no acknowledgement of the new fare, and to her complaint ("quoted $16.26, charged $21.14") to argue she was never given a live chance to decline — consent-by-silence is not consent under RD-5.

The driver's statement in F13 asserts she was told the multiplier, the fare and free cancellation, but F13 is a written statement made after the trip with no call recording, so under RD-5 it cannot outweigh the fare log (F9) or establish her acknowledgement.
The revised estimate in the notice ($22.48, F9) is $1.34 above the $21.14 actually charged (F5/F7); the rider may argue the notice was inaccurate, though SURGE-1 only requires a stated estimate.

notices.text: We have reviewed your dispute: part of the fare is refunded. $4.88 will be refunded to your original payment method. The decision follows Ryde's dispute policy and the trip record.

About this trip's dispute: the rider is being refunded $4.88 to the original payment method.

The notice told the rider free cancellation was available until a time that had already passed when the message was sent — so the option couldn't actually be used. A surge notice has to offer a free cancellation the rider can still take.

No account flag was applied. Please make sure any surge notice you send offers a usable free-cancellation window. The notice defect has been logged on the trip record.
